transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-13
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Park (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Quantaco Head of ML), Arjun Patel (Quantaco Platform Eng), Leah Gomez (Quantaco Data Scientist)

Summary: quick run through of economics from last week's pilot results, digging into tokens per second per dollar, and looking at caching and batching tradeoffs.

[00:00] Maya Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll focus on the cost numbers and the experiments daniel ran overnight and then agree next steps, is that right priya?
[00:08] Priya Singh: yep that's the plan, we've got some PM pressure to understand unit econ before next exec sync so want the tight numbers.
[00:15] Daniel Cho: I ran the replay with 3 different batching configs and one KV cache setting, I have a few slides but I'll just call out the numbers first — baseline hosted model (redwood default, float16) was about 1.2M tokens per dollar for our average prompt mix, with median latency at 180ms.
[00:34] Leah Gomez: 1.2M tokens per dollar sounds good, but our tail latency is what the product team cares about — how does batching impact tail?
[00:42] Daniel Cho: right, so with aggressive batching (max batch size 64, 50ms accumulation) tokens/sec improved ~35% which bumped tokens per dollar to about 1.62M, but p95 latency rose from 180ms to 420ms on our peak windows. We saw an average latency improvement for bulk throughput but tail suffers.
[01:10] Priya Singh: that's the classic tradeoff — how much tail can we tolerate? Our SLAs for chat need p95 < 300ms ideally.
[01:18] Maya Park: one lever is dynamic batching thresholds by route; we can set lower accumulation for chat-like routes and higher for async batch jobs. Redwood supports route-level batching policies.
[01:29] Arjun Patel: can you quantify cost impact if we keep chat routes small and batch only background tasks?
[01:34] Daniel Cho: yes — splitting traffic 70/30 chat/background, and only batching background, tokens/sec/$ for overall footprint falls to ~1.38M (vs 1.2M baseline) but chat p95 stays near 200ms. The net cost savings are still positive (roughly 10-12% lower monthly bill) because background accounts for a lot of tokens. Our spreadsheet shows the math.
[01:58] Leah Gomez: what about caching? we've been told by eng that many requests share similar prefixes so KV/prefix caching could help.
[02:05] Daniel Cho: I ran a quick KV cache experiment with a conservative cache TTL; hit rate in the replay was ~18% using current prompt set, which reduced effective tokens generated by about 15% — that maps to directly lowering tokens billed by similar percent so tokens/sec/$ improved roughly proportional.
[02:28] Priya Singh: 18% hit rate is ... okay. We think with small prompt normalization we can probably get to 25-30% though.
[02:34] Maya Park: yea often small prompt templating bump hit rates. We'll share recommended normalizations (strip timestamps, standardize system messages).
[02:42] Arjun Patel: how do we measure KV cache impact in production to be confident? we need logs / hit metrics.
[02:48] Daniel Cho: Redwood returns cache hit/miss signals in the trace and in the per-route metrics in the console; I can enable extended metrics for your account for the pilot window. That will let you attribute savings to cache hits.
[03:02] Priya Singh: perfect. On quantization — you mentioned model variants?
[03:07] Daniel Cho: we tested 4-bit quant (Q4) vs float16 on the same model family; Q4 reduced memory footprint and marginally improved tokens/sec/$ by ~8% but increased generation variance in a few edge cases. For production we typically recommend running quality evals on a holdout prompt set before switching.
[03:28] Leah Gomez: any guidance on which prompts to use for that eval?
[03:31] Daniel Cho: use high-value prompts that drive business conversions and a representative sample of edge-case prompts — we can share an eval harness and help run A/B.
[03:38] Priya Singh: so putting it together, what's the best immediate plan to improve unit economics while keeping latency acceptable?
[03:44] Maya Park: proposed short plan: 1) enable KV cache and run 2-week replay to measure hit-rate; 2) split routes to aggressive-batch background traffic only; 3) run quantization A/B on a small traffic slice for quality monitoring. If all look good, roll to dedicated capacity benchmark to see further gains.
[04:05] Arjun Patel: how much do we expect from dedicated capacity vs hosted? is it worth the procurement overhead?
[04:10] Daniel Cho: dedicated gives you predictable slots and sometimes better tokens/sec/$ because of fixed GPU utilization and lower per-token overheads; in our ballpark we estimate another 15-25% improvement when you saturate the hardware with steady workloads. But that requires commit sizing and we should validate with a 2-hour benchmark to get real numbers for your traffic mix.
[04:33] Priya Singh: okay that aligns with finance. If dedicated is ~20% cheaper at scale and combined with caching and batching policies we might get to 40% lower unit cost.
[04:43] Leah Gomez: a question about billing: when a cache hit occurs are we billed for the tokens in the prompt or only the generated tokens?
[04:50] Maya Park: good question — Redwood billing counts tokens sent to the model and tokens generated, but prefix/KV cache can avoid recomputation; when the cache returns a stored response we reduce model invocation costs, and the billing on the platform side reflects effective model compute. We'll include a note in the spreadsheet showing line items for prompt tokens vs generated tokens vs cache-saved compute.
[05:10] Arjun Patel: what about warm KV caches on dedicated nodes when we scale up or failover? will there be cold starts that kill hit rate?
[05:18] Daniel Cho: there can be cold caches after scaling events — we recommend sticky routing and pre-warming strategies for critical routes, and we also support persisted cache snapshots for quicker warm-up. We'll document the expected recovery curve.
[05:33] Priya Singh: action items?
[05:35] Maya Park: I'll take sending the cost spreadsheet and recommended quantization configs. Daniel will run the KV cache replay with extended logs and share the hit-rate traces. Arjun will pull the request distribution and peak concurrency. We'll target those due dates this week.
[05:49] Priya Singh: sounds good. Also can you add a row in the spreadsheet showing tokens/sec/$ sensitivity to cache hit-rate increments (e.g., 0,10,20,30%)?
[05:58] Daniel Cho: yes I'll add that sensitivity table.
[06:02] Leah Gomez: and if we go to dedicated, can we do a short reserved slot (like a 2-hour run) to validate numbers before committing?
[06:09] Maya Park: absolutely, we'll schedule that once we have your logs.

Crosstalk / closing notes:
[06:15] Maya Park: ok thanks all, I'll send the spreadsheet and a proposed time for the dedicated benchmark.
[06:20] Priya Singh: thanks everyone.
[06:22] Meeting end.
